summary:
I checked the newest official statement on the Irkutsk case: WHO's Disease Outbreak News, published Oct 10, 2026 (DON620). It says "the authorities further reported that the fatality was not due to plague infection," and WHO lists the cause as "pneumonia of undetermined etiology." WHO also names a "key uncertainty": the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker. In the same report, all contacts stayed asymptomatic and tested negative, WHO found no evidence of ongoing transmission, and WHO advises no restrictions on travel or trade. Two more dated statements came out on Oct 11. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the threat to the US is "extremely low" and that CDC is watching travelers who arrive from the Siberian region. The NYT wrote that Russia still hasn't said what pathogen killed her.

What this means for the radar: the news phase is peaking and will probably fade over the next 3–10 days as Russian measures end. The best openings now are:
- one complete status decoder dated Oct 10, giving both halves (authorities say not plague; WHO says no confirmed diagnosis);
- the CDC "extremely low" US-risk news;
- a new Plague 101 angle that the news makes timely: presumptive versus confirmed plague tests under CDC's case definition, which explains how a diagnosis can stay "undetermined."

The evergreen search questions are still the steadiest bets: person-to-person spread, symptoms, curability, the US count, and pneumonic versus bubonic. Momentum on these is falling slowly across the 8 snapshots (from about 91 to 86).

New emerging items:
- Plague vaccine status. Only preclinical candidates exist, such as UTMB's July 2026 study, and there is no FDA-approved plague vaccine.
- The 2009 Chicago lab-acquired plague case reported in MMWR. Use MMWR's wording exactly: "attenuated" and "might have."
- Madagascar's plague season, which runs September to April.

Two items are rejected:
- Bioweapon, cover-up and family-claim stories, plus "telltale sign" framing.
- Off-focus doom commentary such as the permafrost piece.

Unverified details about the worker, including her name and "broken test tube" accounts, are being passed around online. Leave them out.

candidates.topic: Plague case in Russia: what's confirmed vs reported, as of Oct 10, 2026 (WHO Disease Outbreak News)
candidates.angle: A dated decoder that puts each statement next to the body that made it. Oct 10, WHO: 'the authorities further reported that the fatality was not due to plague infection.' WHO's own framing is still 'pneumonia of undetermined etiology,' and it calls 'the absence of a confirmed diagnosis' a key uncertainty. Contacts stayed asymptomatic and tested negative, and WHO advises no travel or trade restrictions. Never end on the most reassuring line. Include the earlier dated steps (Oct 6, 7, 8, 9), and add Oct 11: CDC called the US threat 'extremely low.'
keywords: did plague kill the russian lab worker
candidates.why_now: WHO's new DON on Oct 10 is the biggest official change since the first reports. Reuters, AP, ABC, the Independent, Al Jazeera and the NYT all ran it Oct 10–11, and most coverage gives only one half of it. Our playbook already names this decoder as the next long-form and a breaking-news Short.

evidence.signal: 'fatality was not due to plague infection' (authorities, via WHO); 'pneumonia of undetermined etiology'; key uncertainty: no confirmed diagnosis; no travel/trade restrictions advised
WHO unsure what caused pneumonia that killed plague-lab worker (Oct 10)
'No plague case' in Siberia, Russia tells WHO as assessments continue

candidates.topic: Plague risk to the US: CDC director calls it 'extremely low' and explains how arrivals from Siberia are monitored (Oct 11, 2026)
candidates.angle: 'Plague and the US: what CDC said on Oct 11.' Quote Director Schwartz word for word: 'we are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low.' Then explain what a port health station at JFK actually does. Say plainly that WHO advises no travel restrictions. End on the urgent-contact line for anyone with a possible exposure and symptoms.
keywords: is plague coming to the us
candidates.why_now: Fox News, GMA and the Hawaii Tribune-Herald (via AP) reported the CDC director's comments Oct 11, and Medical Daily followed the same day. The question US viewers are typing ('is it here?') now has a fresh, citable agency answer. Our format with a place plus an agency number is our strongest proven plague pattern.

evidence.signal: CDC sees low plague risk, monitors Siberia arrivals; 'threat to the United States is extremely low'
CDC measures in place to assess travelers from Russian region
CDC director: 'We are protected' (Oct 11)

candidates.topic: Plague tests explained: 'presumptive' vs 'confirmed' under CDC's case definition, and why a diagnosis can stay 'undetermined'
candidates.angle: Plague 101 made timely by the news. Use CDC's 2020 case definition exactly: PCR, antigen and F1 tests are 'presumptive.' 'Confirmed' means Y. pestis isolated in culture, or a fourfold antibody change in paired serum. Give at most one neutral sentence of context about the news, with no claims about the Irkutsk case itself. Clinician practice ('treat as soon as plague is suspected') is described as what doctors do, never as advice to viewers.
candidates.why_now: The case now hinges on WHO's 'absence of a confirmed diagnosis' and the NYT's 'Russia hasn't said what pathogen.' People are asking how anyone can not know what killed someone, and almost no creators explain how plague testing works.

evidence.signal: 'A key uncertainty… is the absence of a confirmed diagnosis'
A Week Later, Russia Hasn't Said What Pathogen Killed Plague Researcher (Oct 10)

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague: can it spread person to person? CDC: through respiratory droplets during direct, close contact, unlike measles
candidates.angle: A myth correction that answers the search question in the first 10 s. Use the source wording: 'requires direct and close contact' and CDC's 'can sometimes cough droplets.' Compare with measles and COVID by naming both sides. Close on the urgent-contact line.
keywords: can plague spread person to person
candidates.why_now: This is the top search question in 8 straight snapshots, though momentum is easing (91 to 86). Contagion Live's FAQ, the Naked Scientists and the Daily Observer ('global outbreak unlikely') covered it Oct 9–10, so it is still being asked.

evidence.signal: FAQ: Pneumonic Plague (Oct 9)
What is pneumonic plague, and how is it transmitted?

candidates.topic: Plague symptoms: CDC's 4 pneumonic warning signs (fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain) and when to get urgent care
candidates.angle: A plain search answer: 'Plague symptoms: when to get urgent care (CDC).' List all 4 pneumonic signs, give the 1–4 day timing exactly as CDC words it, and briefly contrast with the bubonic swollen lymph node. Tie 'contact a doctor or local health authority urgently' to a possible exposure. No self-diagnosis framing.
candidates.why_now: This has stayed high across 8 snapshots. Searches for symptoms are typically stickier than news searches and keep going after the news fades.

evidence.signal: Pneumonic plague, by the numbers
What to know about the possible pneumonic plague case (Oct 9)

candidates.topic: Plague contacts: what 'monitoring completed' and 'all contacts tested negative' mean, and how contact tracing ends
candidates.angle: 'Plague exposure? What health authorities do next.' Cover tracing, observation for the incubation window, preventive antibiotics prescribed by health authorities, isolation, and the point when monitoring stops. Use settled practice, with Madagascar 2017 as the worked example. On the current case, one dated line: WHO, Oct 10: contacts 'remained asymptomatic and tested negative.' Never suggest self-treatment.
keywords: what happens if exposed to plague
candidates.why_now: Russia has lifted its measures (SCMP, Bloomberg, Kyiv Post), and WHO's Oct 10 DON gave the contact outcome. That raises the obvious question of why monitoring ends when it does.

evidence.signal: 'All contacts remained asymptomatic and tested negative'
Russia lifts plague lab-related quarantine measures

candidates.topic: Is plague curable? CDC: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly'
candidates.angle: Answer the 'no cure' myth with CDC's exact line. Explain why timing matters most for pneumonic plague. No drug names with doses and no stockpiling advice. Close on the urgent-contact line.
candidates.why_now: It reached 102 on Instagram, and the SCMP's 'a cure' explainer (Oct 10) shows the question is still being asked. A rebuilt Short at 35–50 s would also run our pending length test.

evidence.signal: The plague isn't history. Where it still exists, how it spreads and a cure (Oct 10)

candidates.topic: Plague never went away: where it still occurs (DR Congo, Madagascar, Peru, US West), with Madagascar's Sept–April season starting
candidates.angle: 'Plague today: where it still happens (WHO).' Use WHO's endemic-country list, Madagascar's September–April seasonal rise, and CDC's US count copied live at publish time. Keep it calm and focused on prevention. Don't stigmatise any region.
candidates.why_now: PBS/AP ('The plague never went away'), Axios ('where plague strikes most') and India Today all ran this angle Oct 9–10. Madagascar's seasonal window is open now.

evidence.signal: Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the U.S. nearly every year (Oct 9)
Here's where plague strikes most
Madagascar seasonal plague Sept–April; pneumonic case reported Jan 2026

candidates.topic: Plague in the US: how many human cases a year (CDC), pets, fleas and practical prevention
candidates.angle: Our best plague format. Copy CDC's live wording at publish time (on Oct 7–9 it read 'an average of five human plague cases… range 0–17'). Cover pets and fleas, and always add 'follow the label; some dog flea products (e.g. permethrin) are toxic to cats.' Any 2026 state cases must come from state health department releases checked at publish time. Some outlets still quote 'about 7,' so don't use that number.
keywords: how many plague cases in america
candidates.why_now: The CDC director's 'extremely low' comment and the PBS 'US nearly every year' piece revive interest. Searches also show 2026 human cases reported in New Mexico and Arizona (state-level; verify before use).

evidence.signal: Human plague case in Apache County, Arizona (2026, per search; verify with county/state release)
Cases reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year

candidates.topic: Plague vaccine: is there one? No FDA-approved plague vaccine; candidates are still preclinical (e.g. UTMB, July 2026)
candidates.angle: 'Plague vaccine: where things actually stand.' Explain that animal results are not human results, and why antibiotics, not vaccines, protect contacts today. Correct the 'vaccine shows promise amid outbreak' framing: the work is preclinical and isn't tied to the Russian case.
keywords: is there a vaccine for plague
candidates.why_now: The European Medical Journal ran 'Pneumonic Plague Vaccine Shows Promise' on Oct 10. 'Is there a vaccine?' is a natural follow-on search, and few creators answer it properly.

evidence.source: European Medical Journal via Google News
evidence.signal: Pneumonic Plague Vaccine Shows Promise (Oct 10)
Experimental plague vaccines protect against deadly infection in preclinical study (Jul 28, 2026)
Is there a vaccine against plague?

candidates.topic: Lab-acquired plague: the 2009 Chicago case (CDC MMWR), and what it teaches about lab safety
candidates.angle: Settled history from a primary source. Use MMWR's exact terms: the KIM D27 strain was 'attenuated' (never 'weakened on purpose'), and hemochromatosis 'might have' supplied iron. Keep MMWR's recommendation whole: report to the institution and to health-care providers. Do not compare it with, or speculate about, the Irkutsk case. Don't lead with the scientist's name.
candidates.why_now: Céline Gounder's Oct 10 piece and Forbes on biosafety (Oct 10) brought this precedent back. Search interest in 'lab plague' is rising, and few creators cover it accurately. L1 10-12 failed on this exact topic, so stick strictly to MMWR's verbs.

evidence.signal: Fatal laboratory-acquired infection with an attenuated Y. pestis strain, Chicago 2009
Lab-acquired plague: the 2009 Chicago case and the 2026 Irkutsk death

candidates.topic: How labs that study plague keep it contained: biosafety levels (BMBL), protective gear and post-exposure reporting
candidates.angle: A calm explainer on BSL-2 vs BSL-3 for Y. pestis work as set out in the BMBL agent summary (cite the direct page, not the landing page). Cover what labs do after a possible exposure. No claims about what happened in Irkutsk.
candidates.why_now: Forbes, the Washington Post op-ed ('What happened inside Russia's plague lab?') and UnHerd (Oct 11) all push the biosafety angle. Steady over 4 snapshots, with momentum around 70.

evidence.signal: Russian Anti-Plague Laboratory Death Raises Questions On Biosafety (Oct 10)

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague vs bubonic plague (and septicemic): the 3 forms and why only pneumonic passes between people
candidates.angle: Rebuild the dead carousel as a Short that names both sides. Use WHO's 30–60% only as 'a case-fatality ratio for the bubonic type.' Don't widen pneumonic-only facts to all plague.
candidates.why_now: Steady across 5 snapshots. The playbook says to rebuild it as a Short, because the carousel reached 1 account, which was a format problem, not a topic problem.

evidence.source: Health and Me via Google News
evidence.signal: The Black Death Bacterium Still Exists

candidates.topic: Plague and travel: WHO advises no travel or trade restrictions (Oct 10) vs the US State Department's Russia advisory
candidates.angle: Explain what each body actually said and what a travel advisory is versus a health risk rating, with every line dated and attributed. Leave the politics out entirely.
keywords: is it safe to travel plague
candidates.why_now: WHO's Oct 10 'does not advise any restrictions on travel or trade' sits beside the earlier State Department advisory that mentioned suspected pneumonic plague. Central Asian health checks (Times of Central Asia) and Thailand's DDC statement add to the confusion.

evidence.signal: 'WHO does not advise any restrictions on travel or trade related to this event'
DDC: No plague outbreak in Russia (Oct 11)

candidates.topic: Plague history: Black Death (1340s) vs today, and what antibiotics, germ theory and public health changed
candidates.angle: Calm history-to-now framing with a 'Plague'-first title and no doom words. Pairs with the FT's 'Don't panic about the plague' and the Irish Medical Times' 'not the pandemic threat' framing.
keywords: could the black death happen again
candidates.why_now: Several outlets ran history timelines Oct 9–11. Snapshot momentum is drifting down (70 to 66), so this is better as a long-form than a Short.

evidence.signal: Don't panic about the plague (Oct 10)

candidates.topic: Bioweapon, cover-up, 'telltale sign' and family-claim narratives about the Irkutsk death
candidates.angle: Do not cover. It breaks the guardrails on bioweapon and cover-up speculation, on unverified leaked accounts, and on respect for the person who died.
candidates.why_now: Fox, Euronews, BroBible and SBS are pushing these angles. Listed only so downstream agents skip them.
